newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia orders Azeri oil deal annulled-Turkmenistan.
newsitem.headline: Russia orders Azeri oil deal annulled-Turkmenistan.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin agreed to annul a deal signed between Azerbaijan and two Russian oil firms to develop an oilfield in disputed Caspian territory, Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov said on Thursday.

"I discussed with Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) the question of the status of the Caspian and the question of the agreement between Russian companies and Azerbaijan on the Serdar deposit," Niyazov told a news conference after meeting Yeltsin.

The move would ally the Russian and Turkmenistan governments against Azerbaijan in a dispute over a billion dollar deal in the Caspian Sea where former Soviet states and Iran are in a political battle for control of rich underwater reserves.
Niyazov said he and Yeltsin reached broad agreement on the energy-related issues which dominated their Kremlin discussions, a key topic of which was the status of the Caspian.
Disagreement over who owns what beneath the water body is pitting littoral states against each other in a high-profile, high-stakes diplomatic spat.
The deal just annulled concerns a field known as Kyapaz by the Azeris and Serdar by the Turkmens.
Russia's state oil company Rosneft, its largest oil producer LUKoil and the Azeri state oil company SOCAR signed a deal to develop the field last month.
But Turkmenistan complained bitterly about the deal, leading to Rosneft's withdrawal later in July.
The field is estimated to contain around 50 million tonnes of recoverable oil and the deal, which had not been finalised, was reckoned to be worth around $1 billion.

Turkmenistan also lays claim to some or all of two other deposits already under development by the $8 billion Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC) consortium, led by British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil.
Niyazov did not refer to the two fields -- an extremely sensitive issue between Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan because so much money and such huge reserves are involved.

But the diminutive, silver-haired Niyazov, still enjoying a Soviet-style personality cult in the Central Asian republic of Turkmenistan, said Yeltsin would turn his attention to the general question of the status of the Caspian soon.
"Boris Nikolayevich said he would look at the status of the Caspian soon, and I invited him to come to Ashgabat," Niyazov said.
Russia and Iran view the Caspian as a lake, arguing its deposits should be developed jointly. Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan view is as a sea, which should be divided up territorially.
The issue is further complicated by rows between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan over how the Caspian divisions shoud be made.
